title: Here’s the scoop on 32-inch gravel bikes
content:
Cyclist
Here’s the scoop on 32-inch gravel bikes

32-inch wheels have become a hot ticket item, with many brands testing the new wheel size on prototype gravel and XC mountain bikes. As yet, not many have taken the plunge and actually sell 32in bikes, although that looks set to change, and fast.

In general, 32in gravel bikes are being sold by small volume producers, with titanium the favoured frame material, due to the ease of fabrication of a frame with novel geometry relative to carbon. The novelty of the new wheel size allows a frame to command a premium price over alloy as well.

The big wheels are already making their mark in gravel racing though, with Unbound XL won in 2026 by Robin Gemperle on a prototype Scott 32in gravel bike and Leon Kaiser winning the 109km Sea Otter Europe UCI Gravel World Series race in Girona riding a 32in Avona bike.   

So who is selling 32-inch gravel bikes or framesets? Here’s a non-exhaustive list, which is sure to be added to as more brands make 32-inch bikes and framesets available. Lower down, we have a rundown of the pros and cons of the new, larger wheel size.  

Brand selling 32in gravel bikes or framesets

Avona 

German brand Avona is somewhat unique in selling a carbon framed 32in bike, particularly a race-winning one. You can order the Callis 32 from its site in sizes M, L and XL as a frameset, rolling chassis or fitted with a SRAM XPLR AXS groupset. It reckons the bike will fit riders from 165cm up to 201cm and, unusually for a 32in bike, there’s a road-width 68mm BSA threaded bottom bracket shell rather than a wider MTB shell.

There’s a choice of its own Faserwerk 45mm wheels on two different DT Swiss hubsets or Newmen Streem G.62 wheels, fitted with Schwalbe G-One RS Pro 50mm tyres, with Maxxis Aspen ST tyres available from early 2027. It has Boost spacing and clearance for 55mm tyres and also comes in four colours. Claimed bike weights are from 7.78kg.

Baum

The standard Baum DBM is a 700c titanium frameset, but the Australian brand also offers a custom-built 32in upgrade. Baum says the DBM 32 is aimed at riders over 183cm tall. It too has Boost axle spacing, but also has an MTB-style 89.5mm width T47 bottom bracket shell.

Baum claims you can fit 2.6-inch MTB tyres and that Enve’s carbon MTB fork, which it specs, offers enough clearance for the larger wheel size. Baum has also built a bike fitted with a travel-limited Cannondale Lefty Ocho suspension fork.

Chiru Bikes

Chiru Bikes is a titanium specialist based in Hong Kong, but with French roots, with a history in MTB before branching out into gravel. The Chiru Veldt includes a 3D printed bottom bracket and a titanium fork and is available in two sizes: M/L and L/XL. 

The bottom bracket shell is an MTB-style 92mm T47 and it can handle tyres up to 2.25in, with Boost axle spacing. It showed off a striking bike equipped with Biturbo X 32 Safewing six spoke wheels from German brand Bike Ahead at Cycling World Düsseldorf in March 2026.

Mosaic Cycles

Colorado-based Mosaic Cycles’ GT-1 i55 32” is another hand-built, made to order titanium bike and offers 55mm tyre clearance, with Boost spacing and includes a carbon fork. There’s a T47 bottom bracket with gravel chainline. 

The bike features a 3D printed titanium bottom bracket yoke, which allows it to accommodate a 1x groupset with a chainring up to 46t in size and it says that its curved seat tube helps keep the wheelbase short and the ride lively. Mosaic quotes an eight week lead time, but expects to move the bike to its batch-built programme, which should make for faster turnaround.

Nordest

The Nordest Arisco Ti is also a 32-inch frameset made from titanium, in its case from Madrid, Spain. It can handle 2.4in tyres, with a steep seat tube, long reach and slack head tube claimed to make for efficiency climbing and allow fast descents. 

The frame is available in sizes ML and L, which should fit riders from 175cm to 193cm, as well as custom geometry. It has Boost spacing and a road/gravel width 68mm T47 bottom bracket. It’s designed to fit a 444mm length fork, which doesn’t form part of the build. 

Salsa Fargo 32

Salsa sells its Fargo 32 frameset in both steel and titanium, including a carbon fork. It’s unusual for 32in bikes in selling a small frame size, which it says is suitable for riders from 157cm in height. 

There’s 2.4-inch tyre clearance, it can accommodate an 80mm travel suspension fork and is Boost spaced with a 73mm BSA threaded bottom bracket shell. There’s room to fit a 36-tooth chainring.  

Singular Pterodactyl 

Singular’s 32-inch bike, the Pterodactyl, is also made of titanium. It’s sold in sizes L, XL and XXL and Singular says it will fit riders from 178cm in height. Sold as a rolling chassis with a Columbus carbon fork, it has a 73mm T47 bottom bracket and Super Boost rear axle spacing and can fit 2.5in tyres and a 34-tooth chainring.

In the UK, it’s sold with Maxxis Aspen ST 2.25in tyres on Willow AL rims with Hope hubs, in the US with Astral Jester rims on Approach hubs. 

32in gravel bikes: all you need to know

What are the claimed advantages of 32in wheels?

A major advantage claimed for larger wheels is better rollover of trail obstacles. It’s the same argument as when mountain bikes predominantly switched from 26-inch to 29-inch wheels.

The tyre has a shallower angle of attack when it hits a bump, so it’s not deflected upwards so sharply and will carry momentum better, as well as not translating forward motion into upward motion so violently. It’s a larger-scale version of the logic for wider tyres on road bikes.

There’s a larger contact patch with the ground too, due to the larger wheel radius, which also aids traction and control.

The wheel and tyre combined will, in general, be heavier than a comparable 700c wheel/tyre combination, which again helps preserve forward momentum over obstacles and also increases stability, as it’s harder to turn the larger, heavier wheel. 

Finally, 32-inch wheels may be a better choice for tall riders, helping to keep the frame in proportion – more on sizing below.

And what are the disadvantages?

Larger wheels mean more weight and inertia, so a 32in gravel bike, although it may maintain momentum better, may be slower to accelerate and climb than a 700c gravel bike. The stability we just mentioned can also result in a loss of agility to handle more technical ground.

As yet, there are relatively few components available for 32in bikes – again, we’ll dive into this more below.  

32-inch wheels would not be allowed by the UCI in road races under its current rules – and we all know how reluctant the UCI is to change those.

The wheel size first made its mark in XC mountain biking, and the UCI has indicated that it will not ban 32in wheels in MTB races. However, it’s rumoured to be considering a ban on the wheel size in gravel races it regulates, on the grounds that it puts smaller riders at a disadvantage. Most gravel races are outwith the UCI’s remit though, so it has less leverage than for road races.

Who are 32in gravel bikes for?

As mentioned, 32in bikes can appear more proportional for very taller riders and many of the available 32in framesets are sold in larger sizes only.

The larger wheel size makes it increasingly difficult to create a frame to fit smaller riders, due to issues of stack height and toe overlap.

Some brands have successfully sized 32in framesets for smaller riders though, notably Salsa, which sells the Fargo 32 frameset in size S, which it recommends for riders from 157cm to 170cm.

As for how they’re designed to be used, most brands highlight their potential for fast gravel riding and as gravel race bikes, although others highlight their stable handling as an advantage for bikepacking and configure their frames with a full set of mounts.

What other geometry considerations are there?

The bike needs a longer fork to accommodate the larger front wheel, which in turn requires a short head tube. Even so, the stack may be higher than for a 700c frameset, so the ride position may be more upright and less aero, which combines with the larger frontal area of the wheel to potentially increase drag. 

There’s also a need for a longer front centre to reduce the risk of toe overlap, which means a greater frame reach or a slacker head tube angle, or a combination of the two. 

There’s an equivalent lengthening needed for the chainstays to fit the larger rear wheel. Together they can lengthen the wheelbase, resulting in lazier handling than a gravel bike with a shorter wheelbase. Many 32in gravel bikes have a curved seat tube to help tuck the rear wheel under the saddle and reduce the overall wheelbase.

Almost all the 32in framesets above are specced with Boost wheel spacing, as the wider axle allows a wider bracing angle for spokes and so should result in a more rigid wheel; the Singular Pterodactyl has the even wider Super Boost at the rear. 

Some also adopt an MTB-width bottom bracket shell to maintain the chainline within groupset manufacturers’ guidelines. 

What is 32-inch component availability?

Another constraint is the availability of components to fit a 32in bike, although that’s changing fast.

With the wheel size also trendy for XC MTBs, there are already quite a few wheelset options and others in the works, both alloy and carbon. 

Newmen has launched a 32-inch variant of its ultra-deep G.62 gravel wheels and when it launched the 700c Streem G.48, it also said that a 32in variant of the wheels would be coming.

Other brands with 32in wheelsets available include Schmolke, Teravail and Bike Ahead, while other wheelmakers, including Boyd, have showcased prototype 32-inch gravel wheels.

Tyre availability is also increasing. Schwalbe has launched G.One RS Pro and RX Pro tyres in 32in size and 50mm and 55mm widths. Teravail also sells 32in gravel tyres, as well as carbon gravel rims. Other tyre brands including Maxxis, Silca, WTB and Vittoria also sell 32in tyres or have them in the works. 

As gravel bike tyre clearances increase, they’re heading into MTB territory, so 32in MTB tyres are also an option for some 32-inch gravel bikes.

There are a fair few 32in carbon forks on sale, as well as suspension forks for XC MTBs and, as Baum noted, some rigid MTB forks such as Enve’s have the clearance for 32in tyres.

The larger wheel size results in lower gearing being needed for equivalent metres of development, due to the increased tyre circumference, so a 32in bike typically needs to be fitted with a smaller chainring than a 700c gravel bike, which may mean fitting an out-of-series crankset. 

Who is testing the wheel size for gravel?

There are plenty of brands testing the 32in waters, showing off prototypes without committing to their production. Despite its success in Unbound in 2026, Scott labels its 32in gravel bike as ‘a prototype that will never go into production’. 

But other brands we know of with prototype or one-off 32in gravel bikes include Canyon, Ribble, Rose, Genesis, Raymon and Megamo. 

What’s the future for the 32-inch wheel size?

Many of the prototypes mentioned above are likely to come to market over the next few months, although others will be shelved. There will be more mainstream options and bikes are likely to be available at a greater range of prices. 

As the wheel size takes off, there will be more component choices as well, so there should be a greater choice of wheels and tyres to match.

As well as options for larger riders, 32in mullets may take off, with a 32in front and 700c rear wheel, offering the rollover advantage of the larger front wheel with shorter frame geometry and better fit for shorter riders. Despite the extra mass of the larger front wheel, a mullet is still likely to be lighter than a gravel bike with suspension provided by a fork. 

And if 32in gravel bikes turn out to be a bridge too far, 30.5in is also out there. Newmen says it will offer the Streem G.48 in the intermediate diameter in future, while Neuhaus Metalworks in California has built a prototype titanium gravel frameset to test the 30.5in size. Cube is also rumoured to be interested.
